prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical architecture of exceptional formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My case for Cărtărescu rests on the work, not on how the other openings line up. On the common criteria he has an unmistakable voice, a formal and linguistic ambition sustained at very large scale, and real imaginative depth. From public knowledge, Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid turn memory, the body and dream into one metaphysical project. His poetry and shorter fiction suggest range beyond the large novels. Within the framework of Nobel's will, the achievement is a whole body of work rather than a single book. A single-author citation can cover the large-scale visionary novel without difficulty, and the Romanian-language corpus forms a coherent project. I see no timing obstacle. This is a judgment from public knowledge and translated reception, not from independent verification or a full reading.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the case depends heavily on translations of very dense, long Romanian prose, so I cannot confirm that the claimed density and rhythm survive. The scale and recursiveness that make the project impressive may also read as excess, and it is open whether the later novels extend the originality of the earlier ones or mainly elaborate it. If the committee finds that the large novels do not sustain their quality across volumes, the citation would narrow considerably. Adonis has a more securely established historical position, and his very long career raises a timing question that I do not want to dismiss in favor of a candidate who is still adding to his work.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first but flags that the late work may be repetitive or over-extended in places, and she asks whether Adonis's most vital work lies mainly in earlier decades.
responses.response: I share the first worry and cannot settle it without a fuller reading. The citation should rest on the major novels, such as Blinding and Solenoid, rather than on every volume, and the committee should test whether the later books deepen the project or only extend it. Her question about Adonis applies equally to my own preferred candidate, because longevity does not guarantee sustained quality. I place Adonis second because his formal renewal of Arabic poetic language and poetics seems to me decisive for the whole oeuvre, but I accept that the foundational books and the later poetry should be compared directly.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita second, values the formal and moral center of the memorial sequences, and notes that the landscape-scale and public interventions are harder to weigh than the printed poems.
responses.response: I agree that the printed sequences, Purgatory and Anteparadise, should anchor any literary judgment, and that the landscape works are best read as extensions of the poems rather than as an independent claim. That qualification is why I rank Zurita fourth rather than higher. His historical context is powerful, but the committee should judge language and form, not subject alone, and long cumulative poems in translation are difficult to assess. I would want clearer evidence that the achievement holds up in the Spanish text, and I do not think the sequences are less secure than my preferred candidate on formal grounds.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis second as a major formal achievement in remaking Arabic poetic language, and she insists that his contested political and critical positions must not stand in for literary merit.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and would apply it to every candidate, including Wright and Zurita, where political and historical significance can similarly overshadow the prose or the poems. Her point that Arabic poetry loses much of its prosodic and intertextual force in translation also bears on my own limits, since I cannot judge his sound and metre directly. That is a real reason for caution, not a reason to discount the work. I keep Adonis as my first alternative because the formal case appears strong even through partial translation.

responses.point: Palm ranks Anne Carson second for hybrid form and intellectual depth, while questioning how far hybrid, translation-bound and visual works are purely literary and fit the will's 'in an ideal direction'.
responses.response: I did not rank Carson in my own opening list, so my basis for comparison is thinner, and I do not want to dismiss her. Palm's doubt about separating the textual achievement from visual and material format seems to me the right test, and the committee should apply it to Carson as it would to Zurita's interventions. I would need to see the case made on the language and form of the original texts, and on whether the scholarly and translational work can be set apart from the core oeuvre.

uncertainties: Whether the density, rhythm and syntax of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose are conveyed in translation well enough for a committee to judge linguistic achievement.
Whether the later novels sustain or extend the originality of the major earlier ones, or become repetitive or over-extended.
How well the early poetry and shorter fiction are covered in translation, and so how far they can support the citation's claim of range.
For Adonis, how far the sound, metre and dialogue with classical forms can be assessed in translation, and how the poetry and essays should be weighed against each other in a citation.
For Wright, whether a fiction oeuvre of limited size gives enough evidence of sustained quality, and how far oral and Aboriginal English registers can be judged by non-specialist readers.
All assessments rest on public knowledge and the supplied entries; I have not independently verified sources or read the full corpora.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile lists only professional ties to committee colleagues and Academy programmes, and her own practice as a novelist is context, not evidence of any preference.
